Story: There was once, in a barn adjacent to a farmhouse, a small white kitten called Cotton. Cotton resided high above the barn in a warm and comfortable nook where the farmer's horses were accustomed to sleep. Yet Cotton was not solitary in her abode above the barn. She shared her bed of hay with her mother and 5 other sisters. All her sisters were pleasing and fluffy, resembling Cotton in appearance. But she was the sole white kitten among them. The remainder of her sisters were entirely orange, marked with fine white tiger stripes such as Cotton's mother possessed. Her difference of appearance caused Cotton considerable sorrow. She frequently desired to resemble the rest of her family. Thus, upon one day, when Cotton discovered a can of orange paint belonging to the farmer, she employed it to colour herself in imitation of them. When her mother and sisters came upon her, they began to laugh.

"What are you doing, Cotton?!"

"I only wanted to be more like you".

Cotton's mother rubbed her face upon Cotton's and said, "Oh Cotton, but your fur is so pretty and special, like you. We would never want you to be any other way". Thereupon, Cotton's mother lifted her and cast her into a large bucket of water. When Cotton emerged, she was once more herself. Her sisters licked her face until Cotton's fur was entirely dry.

"Don't ever do that again, Cotton!" they all cried. "Next time you might mess up that pretty white fur of yours and we wouldn't want that!"

Thereupon Cotton reflected, "I change my mind. I like being special".

Question: What was the color of Cotton?
Answer:

Story: Once there was a beautiful fish named Asta. Asta lived in the ocean. There were lots of other fish in the ocean where Asta lived. They played all day long. 

One day, a bottle floated by over the heads of Asta and his friends. They looked up and saw the bottle. "What is it?" said Asta's friend Sharkie. "It looks like a bird's belly," said Asta. But when they swam closer, it was not a bird's belly. It was hard and clear, and there was something inside it. 

The bottle floated above them. They wanted to open it. They wanted to see what was inside. So they caught the bottle and carried it down to the bottom of the ocean. They cracked it open on a rock. When they got it open, they found what was inside. It was a note. The note was written in orange crayon on white paper. Asta could not read the note. Sharkie could not read the note. They took the note to Asta's papa. "What does it say?" they asked. 

Asta's papa read the note. He told Asta and Sharkie, "This note is from a little girl. She wants to be your friend. If you want to be her friend, we can write a note to her. But you have to find another bottle so we can send it to her." And that is what they did.

Story: (CNN) -- FBI agents on Friday night searched the Maryland home of the suspect in the recent disappearance of an American woman in Aruba, an agent said. 

The search is occurring in the Gaithersburg residence of Gary Giordano, who is currently being held in an Aruban jail, FBI Special Agent Rich Wolf told CNN. 

Agents, wearing vests that said FBI and carrying empty cardboard and plastic boxes, arrived about 8:40 p.m. Friday. About 15 unmarked cars could be seen on the street, as well as a Montgomery County police vehicle. 

Supervisory Special Agent Philip Celestini, who was at the residence, declined to comment further on the search, citing the active investigation. 

Aruban Solicitor General Taco Stein said earlier Friday that the suspect will appear in court Monday, where an investigating magistrate could order him held for at least eight more days, order him to remain on the island or release him outright due to a lack of evidence. 

Giordano was arrested by Aruban police on August 5, three days after Robyn Gardner was last seen near Baby Beach on the western tip of the Caribbean island. 

Giordano told authorities that he had been snorkeling with Gardner when he signaled to her to swim back, according to a statement. When he reached the beach, Gardner was nowhere to be found, Giordano allegedly said. 

The area that Giordano led authorities to is a rocky, unsightly location that locals say is not a popular snorkeling spot. 

Although prosecutors have continued to identify the 50-year-old American man by his initials, GVG, they also released a photo of a man who appears to be Giordano. His attorney, Michael Lopez, also has said that his client is being held as a suspect in Gardner's death. Lopez has not returned telephone calls seeking comment.

Story: Tommy was a small boy who lived by a big lake by the woods. On a certain day, he observed two little mice gazing at the water. They appeared exceedingly sorrowful. 

"What is wrong?" Tommy asked. 

Mary, one of the little mice, stood. "My brother and I love to see new things. We want to see what is on the other side of the lake. But we do not know how to build a boat to get there." 

Tommy smiled. "I have plenty of toy boats," he said. "They are your size!" 

"Oh, thank you!" said Steve, the other little mouse. "We would be very glad if we could borrow it!" 

Tommy proceeded to his dwelling and came back with a small toy boat. The boat was furnished with a large sail to propel it. Mary and Steve boarded it, and Tommy placed the boat upon the water. 

The boat sailed away across the water. Mary and Steve laughed with joy and experienced great enjoyment in riding the toy boat. 

Before long, they arrived at the opposite shore of the lake. A great many people were enjoying themselves by swimming and splashing in the water. Steve and Mary were delighted to observe all the new things and persons. 

A man cast a ball into the water. It fell near the toy boat. The man's large dog came splashing into the water to retrieve it. The great waves splashed the little boat in every direction. Mary and Steve became exceedingly wet. 

Mary and Steve returned home thereafter. They recounted to Tommy all that they had seen, and they all laughed at the great waves made by the dog. On the morrow, the mice would explore further upon the lake with Tommy's toy boat!

Question: Where'd Tommy live?

Story: Brownie and Spotty, neighbouring dogs, met each day to play together. These two were so attached to one another and played together with such frequency that a path had been worn through the grass of the field between their respective houses. One evening, Brownie's family observed that he had not returned home. They went in search of him without success; by the next week, he was still missing. Curiously, Spotty appeared at Brownie's house alone, barking, whining, and generally pestering Brownie's human family. Being occupied with their own affairs, they merely ignored the anxious little neighbour dog. Ted, Brownie's owner, was constantly disturbed by the angry, determined little dog. Spotty followed Ted about, barking insistently, and then rushing toward a nearby empty lot and back, as if to say, "Follow me! It's urgent!" At length, Ted followed Spotty to a deserted spot, half a mile from the house. There Ted found his beloved Brownie alive, with one of his hind legs crushed in a steel leghold trap. Horrified, Ted now wished that he had taken Spotty's earlier appeals seriously. Then Ted noticed something quite remarkable. Spotty had done more than merely lead Brownie's human owner to his trapped friend. In a circle around the injured dog, Ted discovered an array of dog food and table scraps, which were afterwards identified as the remains of every meal with which Spotty had been fed that week! Spotty had been visiting Brownie regularly, in the hope of keeping his friend alive by the sacrifice of his own comfort. Spotty had evidently stayed with Brownie to protect him from hunger and other perils, and to keep up his spirits. Brownie's leg was treated by a veterinarian, and he recovered. For many years thereafter, the two families watched the faithful friends chasing each other down that well-worn path between their houses.

WAITING. 

The days, lengthening in the sunlight, continued without bringing either that which Romola most desired or that which she most dreaded. No sign came from Baldassarre, and despite the vigilant watch of the Government, no disclosure of the suspected conspiracy was made. Yet other events occurred which affected her deeply, and spanned the spectre-haunted interval of anxiety with active sympathy in present affliction. There came the spreading Plague and the Excommunication of Savonarola. 

These two events served to stay her nascent alienation from the Frate, and to renew her attachment to the man who had disclosed to her the new life of duty, and who now appeared worsted in the struggle of principle against profligacy. For it was not possible for Romola to bear, from day to day, into the dwellings of pestilence and misery, the exalted emotion of a joy that, inasmuch as such anguish endured, she also endured to render some of the bitterness less acute, without recollecting that she owed this sublime moral existence to Fra Girolamo. She could not behold the silencing and excommunication of a man whose difference from the general body of the clergy lay, not in heretical doctrine, nor in his superstitions, but in the fervour with which he endeavoured to render the Christian life real, without feeling herself powerfully attracted to his cause. 

Late in the fervid days of June, the Excommunication, which had arrived from Rome some weeks before, was formally promulgated in the Duomo. Romola repaired to the scene, that the resistance it awakened might strengthen that sympathy with Savonarola which constituted one source of her strength. It presented a memorable contrast to that which she had been wont to behold in that place.

Pierre having departed to attend to the horses, Philip continued his meal; no haste was necessary, for Nevers lay twelve miles distant, and at least four hours must elapse before a party could arrive.

Methinks their intentions were not friendly." 

"I thank you very much for your counsel," Philip said, "and will take it. I know that there are some who would gladly hinder me, in my journey; and if there is, as you say, a risk of their coming here for me, it were as well that I rode farther, although I would gladly have given my horses a night's rest. I thank you warmly for having warned me." 

"Do not let my husband know that I have spoken to you," she said. "He is an honest man, but timid; and in these days 'tis safest not to meddle with what does not concern one." 

Philip awaited two hours, then instructed Pierre to saddle the horses and convey to the landlord his wish to speak with him.

Story: CHAPTER XVII: MACHINATIONS 

"Baby born to woe." 

F. T. PALGRAVE. 

When Anne Woodford began to awake from the constant reflection upon the grief and horror she had left at Portchester, and to feel more alive to her surroundings and less as if they were a kind of dream in which she only mechanically took her part; one thing impressed itself upon her gradually, and that was disappointment. Had the previous shock not blunted all her hopes and aspirations, perhaps she would have felt it sooner and more keenly; but she could not help realising that she had put herself into an inferior position whence there did not seem to be the promotion she had once anticipated. Her companion rockers were of an inferior grade to herself. Jane Humphreys was a harmless but silly girl, not much wiser, though less spoilt, than poor little Madam, and full of Cockney vulgarities. Education was unfashionable just then; and though Hester Bridgeman was better born and bred, being the daughter of an attorney in the city, she was not much better instructed, and had no pursuits except that of her own advantage. Pauline Dunord was by far the best of the three; but she seemed to live a life apart, taking very little interest in her companions or anything around her except her devotions and the bringing them over to her Church. The nursery was quite a separate establishment; there was no mingling with the guests of royalty, who were only seen in excited peeps from the window, or when solemnly introduced to the presence chamber to pay their respects to the Prince. As to books, the only secular one that Anne saw while at Whitehall was an odd volume of Parthenissa. The late King's summary of the Roman controversy was to be had in plenty; and nothing was more evident than that the only road to favour or promotion was in being thereby convinced.

Story: CHAPTER III 

TOM'S JOKE 

"What did you do to him?" inquired Sam, with promptness. 

"Put an advertisement of pills on his back and some other ads. in his text books," Tom answered. "Say, he looks some mad; doesn't he?" 

"I should say yes," came from Stanley.

William Philander drew near with long strides; in one hand he held the poster that Tom had affixed to his back, while with the other he shook his fist in wrath.

"Tom Rover, you've--er--insulted me!" he gasped upon arriving. "You've humiliated me before the whole class! I'll--I'll----" The dandy student, being so full of wrath, could not speak.

"Take a cough drop and clear your throat Billy," Tom suggested, in a cool tone. "Don't get so excited, you might drop dead from heart disease."

"How dare you put that--er--that advertisement of Gumley's Red Pills on my back?" the elegantly attired youth stormed.

"'Gumley's Red Pills for Red-Blooded People,'" Spud quoted from the poster. "Say, they are fine, Willie. Didn't you ever take 'em?"

"No, and I don't want to. I want Tom Ro----"

"Say, if you haven't taken any of Gumley's pills you don't know what you've missed," Spud continued, winking at the others. "Why, there was a man over in Rottenberg who was flat on his back with half a dozen fatal diseases. The doctors gave him just three days to live,--three days, think of it! His wife nearly cried her eyes out. Then along came this Gumley man with a trunk full of his Red Pills for Red-Blooded People. He didn't exactly know if the dying man was red-blooded or not, but he took a chance and gave the fellow sixteen pills, four after breakfast, four after dinner, four after supper and four on retiring, and the next day, what do you think happened? That man got up and went to work, and he's been at his Job ever since."

CHAPTER XXXIV

Arthur stood at the gate as Ruth ascended the steps of Maria's house. She heard the swift clatter of the typewriter, and upon Martin's admission, discovered him engaged upon the final page of a manuscript. Her errand was to ascertain if he would join them for Thanksgiving dinner; yet ere she could raise the matter, Martin launched forth upon the theme that filled his mind.

"Here, let me read you this," he cried, separating the carbon copies and running the pages of manuscript into shape. "It's my latest, and different from anything I've done. It is so altogether different that I am almost afraid of it, and yet I've a sneaking idea it is good. You be judge. It's an Hawaiian story. I've called it 'Wiki-wiki.'"

His countenance was aglow with the fire of creation, notwithstanding that she shivered in the chill of the room and had noted the coldness of his hands at their meeting. She gave close heed as he read aloud, and albeit he discerned but disapproval upon her features at intervals, at the conclusion he inquired:

"Frankly, what do you think of it?"

"I--I don't know," she, answered. "Will it--do you think it will sell?"

"I'm afraid not," was the confession. "It's too strong for the magazines. But it's true, on my word it's true."

"But why do you persist in writing such things when you know they won't sell?" she went on inexorably. "The reason for your writing is to make a living, isn't it?"

Story: CHAPTER V. 

MESSRS. TREAT, JONES, WESTON & DOWD. 

The particular circle of society in which Ben and Johnny moved was thrown into the greatest confusion by the news which was whispered from one to another on the day after those young gentlemen and Paul had taken up their abode at Mrs. Green's. 

Early that morning the most exciting topic of conversation had been Master Spry's misfortune and Tim Dooley's perfidy; and that had hardly begun to be commented upon when the news spread that Ben and Johnny, since the coming of their guest—who was evidently a suspicious sort of a person, as was shown by his clothes and his entire ignorance of the slang of the street—were no longer proud of their neat little bit of real estate, but had made a change which would probably be the means of their financial ruin. That they had been so extravagant as to engage rooms at a regular boarding-house, where they were to spend their substance on three square meals each day, seemed like a reckless disregard of money; and the price which they were to pay for board was stated at various sums from five to ten dollars per week. But that was not the only bit of wonderful news. 

Jimmy Sullivan stated—and he was supported by several others as the time wore on—that Johnny himself had told him that they were to start a regular theatre, and had already engaged a hall, which would be converted into a first-class place of amusement as soon as possible. This would have been regarded simply as a rumor started for the purpose of injuring the credit of these young gentlemen, had it not come so directly from one of the parties concerned, and must therefore be true.

Story: Sean, a dragon, was fond of the colour green. He did not care for golden coins, for they were too yellow. Each day he would go forth to gather green things wherewith to cover his bed of ancient treasure. He would spread grass and clovers and leaves and vines throughout his cave. The other dragons grew worried; when one breathes fire, it is not advisable to sleep among a multitude of plants. They feared that Sean might be hurt. Sean did not think so, but his bed never remained green, and he was becoming weary of doing nothing but tending his bed. One day he went to visit his friend Zarah, and he saw a piece of green set in a golden necklace. "What's that?" he asked. "That's a green stone," she told him. "Sometimes my treasures have them. I don't really like them. They're too green. I like yellow things." "If I bring you yellow things, can I have it?" Sean asked. "Yes you can," Zarah said, "But it has to be treasure, or things that won't catch fire." So Sean went to seek treasure. When he was gone, Zarah told the other dragons. They said that they would trade all their green treasure to Sean as well, so that he might have a safe dragon bed in his cave. Soon Sean had more than enough green stones to cover his bed. Green stones never grow old and brown; they do not catch fire either. So, now everyone was happy.

Story: CHAPTER X 

CAUGHT IN A STORM 

"Did you ever know this Wilbur Poole, Dad?" inquired Ben. 

"Yes, I met him years ago at Aaron Poole's home. But of course he was in his right mind then. Poor chap! I pity him very much." 

"I think we all pity him," answered Dave. "Nobody can be responsible after his mind breaks down." 

"I feel sorry for Nat Poole and his folks," said Laura. "This will give them a great deal of trouble, not to mention the expense." 

"If Wilbur Poole was anywhere around Rayville it might pay to start a hunt for him," suggested Roger. 

"I don't think you'll find him anywhere around here," answered Mr. Basswood. "But it won't hurt to take a look around, if you boys care to take a walk." 

Ben's father departed to dispatch his telegram to Aaron Poole; whereupon all the boys set forth upon a search for the wild man. They traversed the streets of the village and several roads upon the outskirts, yet without success. They encountered three persons who had spoken with the curious individual, and from their accounts Dave and his companions were convinced that the man must have been Wilbur Poole. 

"I guess we'll have to give it up," said Phil, when it was getting late. "I'm tired out. And remember, fellows, we have a hard ride before us to-morrow if we expect to reach Carpen Falls in time to hit the trail for Bear Camp before it gets dark."

Story: A comprehensive apprehension of adolescence within society requires data drawn from diverse disciplines, such as psychology, biology, history, sociology, education, and anthropology. Under all these disciplines, adolescence is regarded as a transitional phase between childhood and adulthood, whose cultural function consists in preparing children for the roles of adult life. It is a period marked by numerous transitions, including education, training, employment and unemployment, together with shifts from one mode of living to another.

Puberty unfolds over an extended period, commencing with an increase in the production of hormones, which in turn induces a variety of physical alterations. It is that stage of life wherein secondary sex characteristics make their appearance and develop—for instance, a deeper voice and a larger adam's apple in boys, and the growth of breasts and more curved, prominent hips in girls—and where a marked shift in the hormonal balance towards the adult state occurs. This transformation is initiated by the pituitary gland, which discharges a surge of hormonal agents into the bloodstream, thereby setting in motion a chain reaction. The male and female gonads are thereupon activated, placing them in a state of rapid growth and development; the stimulated gonads then commence the mass production of the requisite chemicals. The testes chiefly release testosterone, whereas the ovaries mainly dispense estrogen. The output of these hormones increases gradually until sexual maturation is attained. In some cases, boys may develop gynecomastia owing to an imbalance of sex hormones, tissue responsiveness, or obesity.

Within all of these perspectives, adolescence is viewed as a transitional period between childhood and adulthood, whose cultural purpose is the preparation of children for adult roles. It is a period of multiple transitions involving education, training, employment and unemployment, as well as transitions from one living circumstance to another. 

Puberty occurs through a long process and begins with a surge in hormone production, which in turn causes a number of physical changes. It is the stage of life characterized by the appearance and development of secondary sex characteristics (for example, a deeper voice and larger adam's apple in boys, and development of breasts and more curved and prominent hips in girls) and a strong shift in hormonal balance towards an adult state. This is triggered by the pituitary gland, which secretes a surge of hormonal agents into the blood stream, initiating a chain reaction to occur. The male and female gonads are subsequently activated, which puts them into a state of rapid growth and development; the triggered gonads now commence the mass production of the necessary chemicals. The testes primarily release testosterone, and the ovaries predominantly dispense estrogen. The production of these hormones increases gradually until sexual maturation is met. Some boys may develop gynecomastia due to an imbalance of sex hormones, tissue responsiveness or obesity.

Story: CHAPTER XX.

Moving against Captain Grady

Paul and Chet Winthrop were deeply interested in the words uttered by Jeff Jones, the colored member of the horse thieves' gang.

"So you know something of Captain Grady and our uncle, Barnaby Winthrop?" cried Chet, excitedly. "What do you know?"

"Dat's fer you two fellers ter find out--onless yer let's me go," replied Jeff Jones, suggestively.

"You mean you won't speak unless we grant you your liberty?" put in Paul.

"Dat's de way to figure it."

Paul regarded Chet with an inquiring look.

"We can't promise anything until Mr. Dottery gets back," said Chet. "But if you know anything about our uncle you had better speak out, if you wish us to do anything at all for you."

"I won't say a word," growled the colored man.

Chet, vexed, bit his lip.

"Don't you know what it is to have us able to speak a word for you?" said Paul. "Supposing we let Jack Blowfen take you over to the next camp and tell the men that you are a downright horse thief? Would you fancy that?"

Jeff Jones commenced to tremble, for he knew what Paul meant: that he would be lynched within the hour. In that section of the country, at that time, horse stealing was considered almost as grievous as murder.

"No! no! doan let him take me down ter de Fork!" howled Jeff Jones. "Anyt'ing but dat, boys!"

"Well, you, had better talk, then," returned Paul, severely.

"I doan know much, but I'll tell yo' all I do know," said the prisoner, after a short pause, "and yo' is ter do de best yo' can fo' me, promise me dat?"

Story: CHAPTER II. ON A MOUNTAIN PATH 

"Armed men, my lords!" had been Fanfulla's cry. "We are betrayed!" 

They exchanged glances of severity, and wore that grimness which in lesser souls occupies the place of fear. 

Thereupon Aquila rose slowly to his feet; the others rose with him, and made ready their weapons. He softly pronounced a name--"Masuccio Torri." 

"Aye," cried Lodi bitterly, "would that we had heeded your warning! Masuccio it will be, and at his heels his fifty mercenaries." 

"Not less, I'll swear, by the sound of them," said Ferrabraccio. "And we but six, without our harness." 

"Seven," the Count laconically amended, resuming his hat and loosening his sword in its scabbard. 

"Not so, my lord," exclaimed Lodi, laying a hand upon the Count's arm. "You must not stay with us. You are our only hope--the only hope of Babbiano. If we are indeed betrayed--though by what infernal means I know not--and they have knowledge that six traitors met here to-night to conspire against the throne of Gian Maria, at least, I'll swear, it is not known that you were to have met us. His Highness may conjecture, but he cannot know for sure, and if you but escape, all may yet he well--saving with us, who matter not. Go, my lord! Remember your promise to seek at your cousin's hand the gonfalon, and may God and His blessed Saints prosper your Excellency." 

The elder grasped the younger man's hand, and bending his head until his face was concealed by his long white hair, he pressed a kiss of fealty upon it. Yet Aquila was not to be so readily dismissed.

"Armed men, my lords!" had been Fanfulla's cry. "We are betrayed!" 

They looked upon one another with stern eyes, and with that grimness which assumes the station fear would occupy in meaner souls.

"Aye," cried Lodi bitterly, "would that we had heeded your warning! Masuccio it will be, and at his heels his fifty mercenaries." 

"Not less, I'll swear, by the sound of them," said Ferrabraccio. "And we but six, without our harness." 

"Seven," the Count laconically amended, resuming his hat and loosening his sword in its scabbard. 

"Not so, my lord," exclaimed Lodi, laying a hand upon the Count's arm. "You must not stay with us. You are our only hope--the only hope of Babbiano. Remember your promise to seek at your cousin's hand the gonfalon, and may God and His blessed Saints prosper your Excellency." 

The old man caught the young man's hand and, bending his head until his face was hidden in his long white hair, imprinted upon it a kiss of fealty. But Aquila was not so readily dismissed.

Story: CHAPTER XVII.

A grey dimness was creeping upon the schooner when a slight bitter breeze arose from the west, and Dampier commanded them to set the mainsail. 

"I don't like the look of the weather, and I'm beginning to feel that I'd like to see that boat," he said. "Anyhow, we'll get way on her." 

To hoist the mainsail was a relief; the labour imparted a measure of warmth, and the white men, at the very least, had become aware of an increasing unease regarding their comrades in the boat. The breeze had, nevertheless, freshened prior to their setting it, and whitecaps appeared upon the water as the _Selache_ made for the ice. It had undergone some alteration in its formation as they drew near, for considerable masses had broken free and were drifting into open water, whilst the gap had grown perceptibly less wide. The light was by now diminishing swiftly, and Wyllard assumed the helm as Dampier dispatched the man forward. 

"Get the cover off the second boat, and see everything clear for hoisting out," he said to him, and then called to Wyllard. "We're close enough. You'd better heave her round." 

She came round with a lashing of canvas, extended seaward, and returned with her deck sharply inclined and small puffs of bitter spray blowing over her weather rail, for it was certain that the breeze was freshening apace. Thereupon Dampier sent a man aloft into the foremast shrouds, and thereafter regarded Wyllard.

Story: CHAPTER XXVIII. 

A MEETING. 

Approximately a week after the dissolution of the Crooked Creek Company, Harry was riding from Hetertown and had nearly reached the creek on his homeward journey when he encountered George Purvis. 

This constituted their first meeting since the fight, as George had been absent on a visit to relatives in Richmond. 

Upon perceiving George riding slowly toward him, Harry felt exceedingly embarrassed and was vexed by his own embarrassment. 

How ought he to meet George? What should he say, or should he say anything at all? 

He did not wish to appear anxious to "make up" with him, nor did he desire to seem as though he bore malice toward him. If only he knew how George felt about the matter! 

As it was, he wished that he had stopped somewhere upon the road. He had thought of stopping at the mill; why had he not done so? That would have given George time to pass by. 

Both boys appeared to be riding as slowly as their horses would consent to go; yet, when they met, Harry had not half made up his mind what he would say, or how he should say it, or whether it would be better to say anything at all. 

"Hello, George!" said he, quite without premeditation. 

"Hello!" said George, reining in his horse. "Where are you going?" 

"Going home," said Harry, also stopping in the road. 

Thus was the quarrel brought to an end. 

"So you've sold the telegraph?" said George. 

"Yes," said Harry. "And I think we made a pretty good bargain. I didn't think we'd do so well when we started."

Story: CHAPTER VI.—LEO ASSERTS HIS RIGHTS. 

A crowd of performers at once surrounded the pair; as few of them were fond of Jack Snipper, they wondered what Leo would do should the gymnast attack the boy. 

“Call me a braggart, will you!” roared Snipper. 

“Don’t you dare to touch me with that club!” replied Leo calmly. 

“I’ll teach you a lesson!” 

Whereupon, swinging the Indian club above his head, Jack Snipper struck a savage blow at the young gymnast. 

Had the club struck Leo, the boy’s head would have sustained a severe injury. 

However, Leo dodged with great quickness, and the Indian club passed harmlessly through the air. 

“For shame, Snipper!” 

“Do you want to kill the boy?” 

“What harm has he done?” 

Thus the cries continued. 

“Mind your own affairs!” shouted the maddened gymnast. “I’m going to teach the boy a lesson!” 

Again he sprang at Leo. 

But suddenly the Indian club was caught. With a dexterous twist, it was sent flying out of reach across the dressing tent. 

Then, before Snipper could recover, he received a stinging slap full in the face, which sent him staggering backward upon the grass. 

A shout of approval arose. 

“Good for Leo!” 

“That’s right, boy, stand up for your rights!” 

The shout summoned Adam Lambert, the general manager, to the scene. 

No sooner had he appeared than all the performers departed. It was contrary to the rules to fight, and every person present was liable to a heavy fine.

At once a crowd of performers surrounded the pair. Very few of them liked Jack Snipper, and they wondered what Leo would do should the gymnast attack the boy.

Story: Zen (), a school of Mahayana Buddhism, had its origin in China during the Tang dynasty, where it was termed Chan Buddhism. The Zen school was powerfully influenced by Taoism and evolved as a separate school of Chinese Buddhism. From China, Chan Buddhism extended southward to Vietnam, northeastward to Korea, and eastward to Japan, in which country it received the name Japanese Zen. 

The term Zen is derived from the Japanese pronunciation of the Middle Chinese word 禪 (Chan), which traces its origin to the Indian practice of Dhyana ("meditation"). Zen emphasizes rigorous self-control, the practice of meditation, insight into Buddha-nature, and the personal expression of this insight in daily life, with particular regard to the benefit of others. As a consequence, it sets less store upon mere knowledge of sutras and doctrine, and favors direct understanding through zazen and intercourse with an accomplished teacher. 

The teachings of Zen embrace various sources of Mahayana thought, more especially Yogachara, the Tathāgatagarbha sūtras, and the Huayan school, with their emphasis upon Buddha-nature, totality, and the Bodhisattva-ideal. The Prajñāpāramitā literature, and, to a lesser degree, Madhyamaka, have likewise been influential in the shaping of the "paradoxical language" of the Zen-tradition. 

The word "Zen" is derived from the Japanese pronunciation of the Middle Chinese word 禪 () (pinyin: "Chán"), which is itself derived from the Sanskrit word "dhyāna" (ध्यान ), a term that may be rendered, with approximate fidelity, as "absorption" or "meditative state".

Charles VIII having been driven out of Italy, it still remained for the allies to remove all traces of his passage from Naples and to restore the rule of the House of Aragon. For this purpose, they had the aid of Ferdinand and Isabella, who sent an army under the command of that distinguished soldier Gonzalo de Cordoba, known in his day as the Great Captain. 

He landed in Calabria in the spring of 1496; and war broke out afresh through that already sorely devastated land. The Spaniards were joined by the allied forces of Venice and the Church under the condotta of the Marquis Gonzaga of Mantua, the leader of the Italians at Fornovo. 

Lodovico had detached himself from the league, and again made terms with France for his own safety's sake. But his cousin, Giovanni Sforza, Tyrant of Pesaro--the husband of Lucrezia Borgia--continued in the pontifical army at the head of a condotta of 600 lances. Another command in the same ranks was one of 700 lances under the youthful Giuffredo Borgia, now Prince of Squillace and the husband of Doña Sancia of Aragon, a lady of exceedingly loose morals, who had brought to Rome the habits acquired in the most licentious Court of that licentious age. 

The French lost Naples even more easily than they had conquered it; and by July 7 Ferdinand II was able to reenter his capital and reascend his throne. D'Aubigny, the French general, withdrew to France, whilst Montpensier, the Viceroy, retired to Pozzuoli, where he died in the following year.

Among the evening's visitors was Donovan, and he did not hesitate to reprove himself harshly for having been so foolish as to suppose that his old friends might have been involved in any dubious affair. 

"The cashier is about as sore a man as can be found in town," he said, "an' if I ain't way off in my reckonin' he'll be lookin' for another job mighty soon." 

"Does he say anything against us?" Bill asked. 

"He's glum as a fish. Every feller who goes in wants to know where Gus is, an' he keeps out of sight all that's possible." 

"Have you seen Mr. Wright to-day?" 

"No; but I heard he an' that lawyer of yours had a long chin about the business. Say, Bill, by the time you get out of this scrape you'll owe a pretty penny for law, I reckon. Why don't you try to make the company pay it?"

The Story: CHAPTER XX 

A BLIZZARD 

A bitter wind assailed the poplar bluff where George and his hired man, Grierson, were engaged in cutting fuel. Save in the river valleys, trees of any magnitude are of rare occurrence upon the prairie; nevertheless, the slender trunks and leafless boughs were massed together and afforded some slight shelter. Upon the open waste, the cold was well-nigh too severe to face, and George once or twice glanced with anxiety across the snowy levels, in quest of some sign of Edgar, who was expected to have joined them with the team and sledge. It was, however, difficult to discern any distance, inasmuch as a gray dimness narrowed the horizon. George stood, attired in snow-flecked furs, in the centre of a small clearing strewn with rows of fallen trunks from which he was hewing the branches. The task was arduous; his entire body strained with each stroke of the heavy axe, yet it sufficed not to keep him warm, and the wind grew more bitter as night approached. 

"I don't know what can be keeping West," he said after a while. "We haven't seen the mail-carrier either, and he's two hours late; but he must have had a heavy trail all the way from the settlement. I expect he'll cut out our place and make straight for Grant's. We'll have snow before long." 

There stood an empty shack not far distant where, with George's permission, the mail-carrier left letters whenever inclement weather rendered it desirable to abbreviate his round. 

Grierson nodded as he cast his eyes about. The expanse of desolate white prairie had contracted since he had last observed it, the encompassing dimness was encroaching ever nearer, and the ranks of poplar trunks were losing their distinctness of form. Now that the men had desisted from chopping, they could hear the eerie moaning of the wind and the sharp patter of icy snow-drost amidst the withered brush.

CHAPTER VIII. BRUCE AND THE WAR OF INDEPENDENCE.

The position of Edward I. towards France rendered it indeed more desirable for him that Scotland should be independent and friendly than partially subdued and hostile to his rule. While she was hostile, England, in attacking France, always left an enemy in her rear. But Edward believed that by clemency to all the Scottish leaders save Wallace, by granting them considerable appointments and trusting them fully, and by summoning them to his Parliament in London, he might unite England and Scotland in an affectionate union. He repaired the ruins of war in Scotland; he began to study her laws and customs; he hastily erected for her a new constitution, and appointed his nephew, John of Brittany, as governor. But he had overlooked two facts: the Scottish clergy, from the highest to the humblest, were irreconcilably opposed to union with England; and the greatest and most warlike of the Scottish nobles, if not patriotic, were fickle and insatiably ambitious. It is difficult to ascertain how often Robert Bruce had changed his allegiance, and how often the Bishop of St Andrews had taken the oath to Edward. Both men were in Edward's favour in June 1304, but in that month they formed against him a treasonable secret covenant. During the year 1305 Bruce prospered in Edward's service; on February 10, 1306, Edward was bestowing upon him a new favour, little suspecting that Bruce, after some negotiation with his old rival, the Red Comyn, had slain him (an uncle of his was also slain) before the high altar of the Church of the Franciscans in Dumfries. It appears that Bruce had attempted to enlist Comyn in his conspiracy, and had found him recalcitrant, or feared his treachery (February 10, 1306).

Story: At the time of my father's fatal illness, I journeyed a thousand miles from home to attend him during his final days. There were a great many matters requiring attention. The task appeared interminable. I was consumed by loneliness, and I abhorred the silence of the apartment.

However, one evening, this silence was disrupted, for I heard a sound of crying from without. I opened the door and discovered a small cat upon the steps. He was thin and destitute; his appearance resembled my own state of mind. I brought him within and provided him with a can of fish. He consumed it and thereafter almost instantly fell into a deep slumber.

On the following morning, I inquired of the neighbors and ascertained that the cat had been forsaken by his owner, who had departed. Thus, the little cat was there quite alone, as I was myself. As I returned to the apartment, I endeavoured to ascertain what course to take with regard to him. Having something else to care for seemed advantageous; however, upon opening the apartment door, he came running and leaped into my arms. From that moment, it was evident that he had no design of departing. I began to call him Willis, in remembrance of my father's closest friend.

But I am aware that we rescued one another. I may have provided him with a home, yet he bestowed upon me something far more valuable.

The afternoon at Clipstone proved a success. Gillian was in attendance, and each individual discovered congenial companions. "Uncle Redgie was so glad to see the hoops come into fashion again," and Vera and Paula were scarcely acquainted with the game, having always played at lawn tennis; but they were eager to learn, since Uncle Redgie was a very fine-looking retired General, and there was a youth besides, grown to manly stature; and one boy, at home for Easter, who, having no taste for croquet, went with Primrose to show Thekla the tame menagerie, where a mungoose, invariably called Raki raki, was the most recent acquisition. She was likewise shown the kittens of the beloved Begum, and received as a gift Phoebus, a tabby with a sage countenance and a head marked like a Greek lyre, destined to be moved to the Goyle in due course. 

"If Sister will let me have it," said Thekla. 

"Of course she will," said Primrose. "Mysie says she is so jolly." 

"Dear me! all the girls at our school said she was a regular Old Maid." 

"What shocking bad form!" exclaimed Primrose. "Just like cads of girls," muttered Fergus, unheard; for Thekla continued--"Why, they said she must be our maiden aunt, instead of our sister."

Story: Endemism denotes the condition whereby a species is peculiar to a defined geographic location, such as an island, nation, country, or other specified zone, or habitat type; organisms that are indigenous to a place are not deemed endemic if they are found elsewhere. The extreme opposite of endemism is cosmopolitan distribution. An alternative term for a species that is endemic is precinctive, which applies to species (and subspecific categories) that are restricted to a defined geographical area.

The word "endemic" is derived from New Latin "endēmicus", from Greek ενδήμος, "endēmos", meaning "native". "Endēmos" is formed of "en" signifying "in", and "dēmos" signifying "the people". The term "precinctive" has been suggested by certain scientists, and was first employed in botany by MacCaughey in 1917. It is equivalent to "endemism". "Precinction" was perhaps first used by Frank and McCoy. "Precinctive" appears to have been coined by David Sharp when describing the Hawaiian fauna in 1900: "I use the word precinctive in the sense of 'confined to the area under discussion' ... 'precinctive forms' means those forms that are confined to the area specified." That definition excludes artificial confinement of examples by humans in distant botanical gardens or zoological parks.

Physical, climatic, and biological factors can contribute to endemism. The orange-breasted sunbird is exclusively found in the fynbos vegetation zone of southwestern South Africa. The glacier bear is found only in limited places in Southeast Alaska. Political factors may play a part if a species is protected, or actively hunted, in one jurisdiction but not another.

The extreme opposite of endemism is cosmopolitan distribution. Physical, climatic, and biological factors can contribute to endemism. The orange-breasted sunbird is exclusively found in the fynbos vegetation zone of southwestern South Africa. Paul and Arthur shared a bachelor residence in Mayfair; that is to say, Paul had purchased it and was the sole proprietor, while Arthur made use of it whenever he could obtain leave from his regiment. It was here that Paul discovered his brother upon the morning of his arrival in London.

"I wish you would let a fellow know what time you were coming," Arthur said, rather peevishly, but with an attempt at a smile. "I didn't expect you till evening, so I was having a shack before dressing. I was late last night!" 

Paul banished his gravity, so far as was possible, and stood with his hands in his pockets, leaning against the mantel-piece. He heartily disliked the part of mentor, and did not wish to play it unless he were obliged. 

"It was beastly early to get up," he said, "but the connection at Normanton is so much better. One has to wait two hours by the late train, and Normanton is such a hole. I don't know that I should have come up to town at all, just yet," he continued after a slight pause, "only that I'm on the committee at the club this term, you know, and I haven't attended a single meeting yet. Besides, I promised Westover to put him up this time, and the half-yearly meeting's to-morrow, you know. Got any engagement? If not, you might dine with me there. Always a full night election time, you know!"

Story: Writing articles about films for The Front Page was my first proper job. Prior to that, I had conducted some reviewing—novels for other newspapers, films for a magazine, and any task I was requested to perform for the radio. Thus it was that I became acquainted with Tom Seaton, the inaugural arts editor of The Front Page, who had likewise contributed to television. He engaged me; however, Tom was not primarily a journalist, or he would assuredly have been more circumspect in the selection of his staff.

Initially, his notion was that a group of critics should attend to those art forms which did not demand specialized knowledge: books, television, theatre, film, and radio. A weekly luncheon was proposed, at which we would select from the artistic material that Tom had determined we should review, though guests would also be invited to render the occasion more social.

The entire affair seemed like a dream at the time: a new newspaper, and I was a member of the team. It appeared exceedingly improbable that a newspaper could be introduced into a market already well supplied. It seemed just as plausible that a millionaire desired to assist me personally and was feigning to employ me. Such was the extent of my want of self-confidence.

Tom's original plan for a team of arts critics never came to fruition. It was a sound idea, but we did not assemble as intended, and thus all business was transacted by telephone. It transpired, moreover, that the general public preferred to associate a reviewer with a single subject area; accordingly, I selected film. Without Tom's initial impetus, however, we should scarcely have devised the present arrangement, whereby I compose an extended weekly article, usually upon a single film.

The space afforded to me permits the broadening of my argument—or, in a dull week, compels me to fabricate something from nothing. But what, then, is my role in the public arena? I assume that people select which films to attend on the basis of the stars, the publicity, or the director. If, therefore, a film review is not truly a consumer guide, what is it? I certainly do not feel that I have a responsibility to be 'right' concerning a motion picture. Nor do I think that there should be a fixed number of 'great' and 'bad' films each year. All that I have to do is to advance an argument. I am not a judge, nor would I wish to be.

Story: (Financial Times) -- While most consumer goods companies are seeking opportunities in China, domestic condom maker Safedom is going in the opposite direction -- seeking European partners or acquisitions as part of a bid to go global.

Brian Fu, chief executive, was in the UK last week "meeting potential partners and acquisitions". Funding for any deal will either come from existing shareholders, bank loans or possibly through an overseas stock market listing, he said. 

Despite the size of the market on its own doorstep -- and added attraction of a government-mandated one-child policy -- Safedom sees its future on the international stage. It reckons its virus-proof latex condoms will enable it to compete alongside the global players such as Durex, now part of Reckitt Benckiser, and Ansell of Australia. 

However, Mr Fu said that the strength of his company -- whose range includes Beautiful Girl, Take Me and Green Lemon -- was in manufacturing and technology, and going global required bringing in branding and marketing expertise. 

Sales outlets and channels are also likely to vary from China, where half of all condoms are bought by women. 

"We think we have good leading edge technology and a good management team. What we lack is the branding part: we are not well known," Mr Fu said.

WHAT ELSA SAW IN THE MOONLIGHT

As soon as he had regained sufficient strength, accompanied by Martin, he journeyed to Leyden, which it was now safe for him to visit, since the Spaniards had been driven from the town.

How his young heart swelled as, still limping somewhat and pale from his recent illness, he approached the well-known house in the Bree Straat, the home which sheltered his mother and his beloved. Presently he would behold them again, for word had been brought to him that Lysbeth was out of danger, and that Elsa was still nursing her.

Lysbeth he found, indeed, transformed into an aged woman by grief and sore sickness, but Elsa he did not find. She had vanished. On the previous night, she had gone forth to take the air, and had returned no more. What had become of her, none could say. WHAT ELSA SAW IN THE MOONLIGHT 

It may be recalled that, some weeks before the forced marriage of Elsa at the Red Mill, Foy, upon their escape from the Gevangenhuis, had been borne upon the bare back of Martin to the refuge of Mother Martha's lair in the Haarlemer Meer. Here he lay ill for many days, since the sword-cut in his thigh had festered so grievously that his life was once threatened by gangrene; but, in the end, his own strength and robust constitution, aided by Martha's simples, effected a cure. So soon as he was strong once more, accompanied by Martin, he travelled to Leyden, which it was now safe for him to visit, since the Spaniards were driven from the town. 

How his young heart swelled as, still limping somewhat and pale from recent illness, he approached the familiar house in the Bree Straat, the abode that sheltered his mother and his beloved. Presently he would see them again, for word had been brought to him that Lysbeth was out of danger, and Elsa must still be nursing her. 

Lysbeth he found indeed, transformed into an old woman by grief and sore illness, but Elsa he did not find. She had disappeared. On the previous night she had gone forth to take the air, and returned no more. What had become of her none could say. The whole town spoke of it, and his mother was half-maddened with anxiety and dread, dread of the worst.

He was a wight of high renown, And thou art but of low degree; 'Tis pride that pulls the country down-- Then take thine auld cloak about thee. SHAKESPEARE. 

The canoe did not reach the mouth of the river until near evening of the third day of its navigation. It was not so much the distance, though that was considerable, as it was the obstacles that lay in the way, which brought the travellers to the end of their journey at so late a period. As they drew nearer and nearer to the place where Gershom had left his wife and sister, le Bourdon detected in his companion signs of an interest in the welfare of the two last, as well as a certain feverish uneasiness lest all might not be well with them, that said something in favor of his heart, whatever might be urged against his prudence and care in leaving them alone in so exposed a situation. 

"I'm afeard a body don't think as much as he ought to do, when liquor is in him," said Whiskey Centre, just as the canoe doubled the last point, and the hut came into view; "else I never could have left two women by them-selves in so lonesome a place. God be praised! there is the chiente at any rate; and there's a smoke comin' out of it, if my eyes don't deceive me! Look, Bourdon, for I can scarcely see at all." 

"There is the house; and, as you say, there is certainly a smoke rising from it"

It must not be supposed that such a history of Guy's mind was expressed by himself, or understood by Mrs. Edmonstone; but she saw enough to guess at his character, perceive the sort of guidance he needed, and be doubly interested in him. Much did she wish he could have such a friend as her brother would have been, and hope that nothing would prevent a friendship with her nephew. 

The present question about the horse was, she thought, unfortunate, since, though Guy had exercised great self-denial, it was no wonder Philip was annoyed. Mr. Edmonstone's vexation was soon over. As soon as she had persuaded him that there had been no offence, he strove to say with a good grace, that it was very proper, and told Guy he would be a thorough book-worm and tremendous scholar, which Guy took as an excellent joke. 

Philip had made up his mind to be forbearing, and to say no more about it. Laura thought this a pity, as they could thus never come to an understanding; but when she hinted it, he wore such a dignified air of not being offended, that she was much ashamed of having tried to direct one so much better able to judge. On his side Guy had no idea the trouble he had caused; so, after bestowing his thanks in a gay, off-hand way, which Philip thought the worst feature of the case, he did his best to bring Hecuba back into his mind, drive the hunters out of it, and appease the much-aggrieved William of Deloraine.

Story: CHAPTER XIII. 

THE LETTER. 

There could be no question that the company of Ninety-four were highly delighted by the news which Seth had brought concerning his progress. 

It was as though each man felt himself personally complimented by Mr. Fernald for advancing the amateur so rapidly; and all united in the declaration that "Josh was a right good fellow." 

Seth was in the highest degree excited. He had expected that his friends of Ninety-four would be pleased to learn of his good fortune, but he had never fancied that they could be so deeply interested; and now he began to understand what a gloom might be cast over the company should he fail in this attempt to gain a foothold in the Department. 

'Lish Davis would not be content until the boy had given an exhibition of what he had learned in the matter of gymnastic exercises during the morning; and when this had been brought to a close amid the applause of all present, the driver said, in a tone of satisfaction: 

"You're getting on in great shape, Amateur, and if nothing happens to give you a pull-back, ought'er be well up in the drill 'twixt now and a year from to-day. Josh Fernald has the name of being precious hard on them as comes under him for instruction; but I've always allowed he'd boost along mighty fast any one who struck his fancy. He must have seen that you were in earnest, young fellow, for when I talked with him the best promise I could get was that he'd look you over in the course of a month or two."

Question: To what degree was Seth excited?

Story: CHAPTER XXVI 

THE JUDGMENT OF DOMITIAN 

Two hours having elapsed, Caleb, in a ferment of rage, sat brooding in the office adjoining the warehouse he had leased. At that instant, he harboured but a single desire—to put to death his successful rival, Marcus. That Marcus had escaped and returned to Rome was beyond all question. He, one of the wealthiest patricians in that city, had furnished the enormous sum which enabled old Nehushta to purchase the coveted Pearl-Maiden in the slave-ring. Thenceforth, his newly acquired property had been conveyed to this house, where he awaited her arrival. Thus, then, was the end of their long rivalry; for this had Caleb fought, toiled, schemed, and suffered. Rather than permit such an outcome, in that dark hour of his soul, he would have seen her cast to the foul Domitian, for Domitian, at least, she would have hated, whereas Marcus, as he knew, she loved.

Now, there remained nothing but revenge. Revenge he must have, but by what means? He might follow Marcus and murder him; only then his own life would be placed in jeopardy, since he knew well the fate that awaited the foreigner, and most especially the Jew, who dared to lift his hand against a Roman noble. Moreover, if he hired others to do the work, they might bear witness against him. Now, Caleb did not wish to die; life seemed the only good that he had left. Furthermore, while he lived, he might still win Miriam—after his rival had ceased to live. Doubtless, then, she would be sold with his other slaves, and he could buy her at the rate such tarnished goods command. No, he would do nothing to run himself into danger. He would wait, and watch his opportunity.

Story: My trip with my sister and my daughter to Manhattan wedding gown(,) shop, cannot be understood without further focusing on Marina, my 14-year-old daughter Ive asked to try on dresses. 

This was the girl I took to Kleinfeld, the fancy store featured on the television program Say Yes to the Dress. As the trip approached, I asked Marina if she was excited. Sure, Mom. shed say, shrugging. Marina was more excited about getting a tattoo on her ankle to represent my fight with ALS than trying on $ 10,000 wedding gowns. 

My sister, Stephanie, had arranged for a car with a wheelchair lift to drive us from the hotel to Kleinfeld. The car driver wheeled me in. 

At Kleinfeld with flower arrangements ten feet high, I felt like rolling into a dream. "Wow!" I said. I was wearing a new black outfit. Marina wore jean shorts, a sleeveless shirt, and sneakers. _ . The kind Kleinfeld ladies pointed out rooms like tour guides, naming the designers one by one on display: Alita Grham, Pnina Tornai... With Marina walking beside me, Stephanie pushed my chair up and down rows and rows of dresses that made Princess Diana's dress look modest. 

Marina didn't say a word. We turned a corner into the storage room, where hundreds of dresses hung in plastic protector sleeves. Marina and I were overwhelmed. 

"Want to try one on ?" I said, touching Marina's hand. 

"OK," Marina said in her sharp, unsure voice. 

"Tell them the style you'd like." 

Marina stood silent. I felt bad for bringing her, for forcing such an adult experience on a child. 

Marina picked an A-line dress. Or, more precisely, the ladies of Kleinfeld picked it for her. Marina was too shocked to do more than nod. As she took the gown into the dressing room, I tried not to think of my little girl on her wedding day or of her as a baby in my arms. I tried not to think of her with her own baby in her arms one day. 

I tried not to think of Marina right now, embarrassed by her mother's plans, by things she could not and should not yet understand. 

I am leaving money in my will for Marina's wedding dress. Stephanie has promised to bring her back to Kleinfeld to purchase it. 

"No pure white!" I said to Stephanie. "Ivory. Not too much tulle . Think lace." 

"Think royalty when picking a dress," I advised Steph as we waited outside the dressing room. "Think Princes Kate. Elegant. Think long sleeves. They make dresses more formal." 

Marina came out, sleeveless, flared . She looked like a 14-year-old girl in the middle of a giant cupcake. 

"I don't like the loose gown." she said. 

That's my girl! 

"How about trying on one with long sleeves?" I asked her. 

The ladies brought out a dress with long lace sleeves, an Empire collar, a ruched fitted waist, and a long, smooth silk skirt. 

Marina disappeared into the dressing room. When the door opened, she looked a foot taller and a decade older. I could clearly see the beautiful woman she will be one day. I simply stared. 

What do you do when you glimpse a moment you will not live to see? 

I dipped my head. Breathe, I told myself. I looked up. I smiled. Marina smiled back. 

I worked my tongue into position to speak. "I like it," I said. 

In that dress, Marina stood straight, shining brightly, and tall. 

"You are beautiful," I whispered, my tongue barely cooperating. I don't know if she heard me. We took some photos. And moved on. A memory made.

Story: CHAPTER VIII

Five minutes after Paula had departed, and punctual to the moment, with the four telegrams disposed of, Dick entered a ranch motor car in company with Thayer, the purchaser from Idaho, and Naismith, the special correspondent of the _Breeders' Gazette_. Wardman, the manager of the sheep, joined them at the corrals, where several thousand young Shropshire rams had been gathered for inspection.

There was scant need for discourse. Thayer was considerably disappointed by this, for he considered that the acquisition of ten carloads of such costly animals was of sufficient moment to warrant abundant conversation.

"They speak for themselves," Dick had assured him, and turned aside to give data to Naismith for his impending article on Shropshires in California and the Northwest.

"I wouldn't advise you to bother to select them," Dick told Thayer ten minutes later. "The average is all top. You could spend a week picking your ten carloads and have no higher grade than if you had taken the first to hand."

This composed presumption that the transaction was already concluded so disquieted Thayer that, together with the certain awareness that he had never encountered so superior a quality of rams, he was provoked into altering his order to twenty carloads.

As he related to Naismith, after they had returned to the Big House and whilst they chalked their cues to resume the interrupted game:

"It's my first visit to Forrest's. He's a wizard. I've been buying in the East and importing. But those Shropshires won my judgment. You noticed I doubled my order. Those Idaho buyers will be wild for them. I only had buying orders straight for six carloads, and contingent on my judgment for two carloads more; but if every buyer doesn't double his order, straight and contingent, when he sees them rams, and if there isn't a stampede for what's left, I don't know sheep. They're the goods. If they don't jump up the sheep game of Idaho ... well, then Forrest's no breeder and I'm no buyer, that's all."

IN NORWAY AT LAST 

Dave was, it must be confessed, startled. It was one matter that Roger should be missing, but quite another that his companion should be absent and the berth made up as though it had never been occupied. 

"He went to bed--I saw him go," muttered the boy from the country to himself. "Am I dreaming, or what can the matter be?" 

The more Dave considered the affair, the more puzzled he became. He dressed with all haste, putting on his clothing and shoes. Thereupon, he opened the stateroom door and proceeded into the passageway that led to the main saloon. 

A dim light burned outside, and no one seemed to be in sight. Dave gazed eagerly up and down the passageway, and even stepped to one corner. He then proceeded to the main saloon, with its large sofas, easy-chairs, and grand piano. Not a soul was visible anywhere. 

"Well, if this isn't the queerest yet," he murmured, and pinched himself, to assure himself that he was not dreaming. He paced from one end of the saloon to the other, and then set out for the stairs that led to the deck. 

At that moment, a violent gust of wind struck the vessel, causing it to rock. Dave was thrown upon his side and fell headlong over the end of a sofa. As he descended, he heard several cries, one in a voice that seemed familiar to him.

Story: CHAPTER XXX.

THE MEETING FOR RAIN.

Meanwhile, the Auld Lichts were assembled in the church, awaiting their minister; and it was a full meeting, because nearly every well in Thrums had been scooped dry by anxious palms. Yet not all were present to ask for God's rain upon themselves. Old Charles Yuill sat in his pew, after having dreamed thrice that he would break up with the drought; and Bell Christison had come, though her man lay dead at home, and she thought that it could matter no more to her how things went in the world.

One who did not love that little congregation would have said that they were waiting placidly. But probably so simple a woman as Meggy Rattray could have led one to suppose that, because her eyes were downcast, she did not notice who put the three-penny-bit in the plate. A few men were unaware that the bell was working overtime, most of them farmers with their eyes upon the windows, but all the women, at least, were wondering. They knew better, however, than to bring their thoughts to their faces, and none sought to catch another's eye. The men-folk looked heavily at their hats upon the seats in front. Even when Hendry Munn, instead of marching to the pulpit with the big Bible in his hands, came as far as the plate and signed to Peter Tosh, elder, that he was wanted in the vestry, one could not have guessed how every woman there, except Bell Christison, wished she was Peter Tosh. Peter was so taken aback that he merely gaped at Hendry, until suddenly he knew that his five daughters were furious with him, when he dived for his hat and staggered to the vestry with his mouth open. His boots cheeped all the way, but no one looked up.

The revolution of Todos Santos had, to all appearances, been carried out as peacefully as the gentle Liberator of Quinquinambo could have wished. A surging mob of vacant and wondering peons, bearing a singular resemblance to the wild cattle and horses which intermingled with them in blind and unceasing movement across the Plaza and up the hilly street, and seemingly as incapable of self-government, were alternately dispersed and stampeded or allowed to gather again as occasion required. Some of these heterogeneous bands were afterwards found, the revolution having been accomplished, gazing stupidly on the sea, or ruminating in bovine wantonness on the glacis before the Presidio. 

Eleanor Keene, who, with her countrywomen, had been hurried to the refuge of the Mission, was more disturbed and excited at the prospect of meeting Hurlstone again than by any terror of the insurrection. Yet Hurlstone was not there, and Father Esteban received her with a coldness which she could not attribute entirely to her countrymen's supposed sympathy with the insurgents. When Richard Keene, who would not leave his sister until he had seen her safe under the Mission walls, ventured at her suggestion to ask after the American recluse, Father Esteban replied dryly that, being a Christian gentleman, Hurlstone was the only one who had the boldness to seek out the American filibuster Perkins, on his own ship, and remonstrate with him for his unholy crusade. For the old priest had already become aware of Hurlstone's blunder, and he hated Eleanor as the primary cause of the trouble; but for her, Diego would be still with him in this emergency.

Story: ChiChi weighs only 13 pounds. "He's so tiny,I can carry him with one hand," says Mary Lane."Most people see him and think he's useless." 

But last October,ChiChi proved to be more than just a pretty face. Mary and her husband,Rick,were relaxing on the beach one afternoon while on vacation in North Carolina's Outer Banks.As usual,ChiChi was lying on his blanket in his own little beach chair. 

"We had our noses buried in books,"recalls Rick,"when suddenly the dog became extremely uneasy. His bark was different from anything we had heard before.And he would not let us ignore him." 

ChiChi ran back and forth in front of his chair as if to run down the beach.The Lanes sat up to see two elderly women in the ocean,about 100 yards down the beach and 10 feet off shore.One was on her back,her head under the waves.The other was struggling hard to keep her friend's head above the surface. 

The Lanes rushed across the sand and into the surf. Rick went to the woman in danger of drowning,while Mary held fast on to the other one and pulled her up on the beach."Then I went back to help Rick," Mary says."The sand dropped off steeply,and a riptide was beating the woman under. She was completely helpless." 

Not getting well from recent knee surgery,the woman had been unable to turn over or push herself up."Her friend had been in danger too," Mary says."The waves were pushing her around. There's no way she could have held on much longer." 

The women hadn't called out for help. "They were struggling so hard that there was no time for screaming," Mary recalls."But ChiChi had sensed their danger." 

Duty done,ChiChi was back in his chair,asleep,by the time the two women were on dry ground and the Lanes had returned to their blankets.Luckily,the women were fine,though shaken.They thanked the Lanes for saving their lives. 

Back home in Greensboro,North Carolina,the Lanes ordered a special collar with the words "Hero Dog" on it.

Story: ChiChi weighs but 13 pounds. "He's so tiny,I can carry him with one hand," says Mary Lane."Most people see him and think he's useless."

ChiChi ran to and fro in front of his chair, as if to hasten down the beach. The Lanes sat upright to behold two elderly women in the ocean, about 100 yards distant along the beach and 10 feet from the shore. The Lanes hastened across the sand and into the surf. Rick proceeded to the woman in peril of drowning, while Mary held firmly to the other and drew her up upon the beach. Recovering but slowly from recent surgery upon the knee, the woman had been unable to turn herself or to raise herself up. "Her friend had been in danger too," Mary says."The waves were pushing her around. There's no way she could have held on much longer." 

The women had not cried out for assistance. "They were struggling so hard that there was no time for screaming," Mary recalls."But ChiChi had sensed their danger." 

Having performed his duty, ChiChi was back in his chair, asleep, by the time the two women had reached dry land and the Lanes had returned to their blankets. Fortunately, the women were unhurt, though much shaken. They expressed their gratitude to the Lanes for having saved their lives. 

Upon their return to Greensboro, North Carolina, the Lanes procured a special collar bearing the words "Hero Dog".

Story: CHAPTER II 

THE RULERS OF FRANCE 

A great bustle prevailed in the corridors and kitchens of the old château. M. le Chef, the only true rival of the immortal Vatel, was in white cap and apron; calm and self-possessed as a field-marshal at the moment of victory, and surrounded by a host of scullions and wenches, he directed the operations of dishing-up, which constituted the crowning glory of his arduous labours. Pies and patties, haunches of venison, trout and carp from the Rhine, were placed upon dishes of gold and silver, and adorned with tasteful ornaments of a truly architectural beauty and monumental proportions. These were then handed over to the footmen, who, resplendent in gorgeous liveries of scarlet and azure, hurried along the marble passages, carrying the masterpieces of culinary art to the banqueting-hall beyond; whilst the butlers, more sedate and dignified in sober garb of puce or brown, stalked along in stately repose, bearing the huge tankards and crystal jugs. 

All of the best that the fine old Château d'Aumont could provide was being requisitioned that night, since M. le Duc and Mlle. Lydie, his daughter, were giving a farewell banquet to Charles Edward Stuart, by the grace of God—if not by the will of the people—King of Great Britain and Ireland and all her dependencies beyond the seas. 

For him speeches were made, toasts drunk, and glasses raised; for him the ducal veneries had been ransacked, and the ducal cellars shorn of their most ancient possessions; for him M. le Chef had raged and stormed for five hours, expending the sweat of his brow and the intricacies of his brain; for him the scullions' backs had smarted, and the wenches' cheeks had glowed—all to do honour to the only rightful King of England, about to quit the hospitable land of France in order to conquer that island kingdom which his grandfather had lost.

Story: CHAPTER VI 

At approximately five o'clock in the afternoon, Ephraim was seated in his shirt-sleeves by the window of his room, whilst Cynthia read aloud to him an article from a Washington paper, which had been sent by his friend, Mr. Beard. The article concerned the war, as was to be expected. There came a knock at the door, and Cynthia opened it to find a colored hall-boy holding a roll in his hand. 

"Mistah Ephum Prescott?" he said. 

"Yes," answered Ephraim, "that's me." 

Cynthia closed the door and handed him the roll; Ephraim, however, received it as though he feared its contents. 

"Guess it's some of them war records from Amasy," he said. 

"Oh, Cousin Eph," exclaimed Cynthia, excitedly, "why don't you open it? If you don't I will." 

"Guess you'd better, Cynthy," he said, extending it to her with a trembling hand. 

Cynthia opened it, and drew forth a large document adorned with seals, printing, and signatures. 

"Cousin Eph," she cried, holding it under his nose, "Cousin Eph, you're postmaster of Brampton!" 

Ephraim regarded the paper, but his eyes swam, and he could discern only a dancing, bronze seal. 

"I want to know!" he exclaimed. "Fetch Jethro." 

But Cynthia had already departed upon that errand. As it happened, she encountered Jethro in the hall directly outside Ephraim's door. Ephraim rose to his feet; it was exceedingly difficult for him to realize that his troubles were at an end, and that he was to earn his living at last. He looked at Jethro, and his eyes became filled with tears. "I guess I can't thank you as I'd ought to, Jethro," he said, "leastways, not now."

It is exceedingly probable that one might have searched throughout New York City that night and not discovered a happier household than that of Mrs. Green's. The good Mrs. Green alternately laughed and wept, until she appeared to realize that such nervousness was not altogether suitable to the occasion, and then she occupied herself with reading one of the papers Ben had brought home. 

Master Treat had devoted so much time to the good work which he had carried through with such success, and then had given so much greater attention to the boy he intended to surprise than to the sale of his wares, that, instead of assisting Johnny as had been his purpose when he took some of his papers to sell, he proved a hindrance, with the result that Mrs. Green had three evening papers to read, while Messrs. Jones and Treat had been "stuck" with precisely that number.

Story: The Achaemenid Empire, likewise styled the First Persian Empire, was an empire seated in Western Asia, founded by Cyrus the Great. At its greatest extent it reached from the Balkans and Eastern Europe proper on the west to the Indus Valley on the east; it was among the largest empires in recorded history, covering 5.5 million square kilometres, and exceeded any empire that had preceded it. It is likewise distinguished for its successful model of a centralised, bureaucratic administration, maintained through satraps under the King of Kings; for the construction of such infrastructure as road systems and a postal system; for the employment of an official language across its territories; and for the development of civil services and a large professional army. The successes of the empire inspired analogous systems in later states. It is noted in Western history as the adversary of the Greek city-states during the Greco-Persian Wars, and for the emancipation of the Jewish exiles in Babylon.

By the seventh century before Christ, the Persians had settled in the southwestern portion of the Iranian Plateau, in the region of Persis, which came to be their homeland. From this region Cyrus the Great advanced to defeat the Medes, Lydia, and the Neo-Babylonian Empire, thereby establishing the Achaemenid Empire. Alexander the Great, an ardent admirer of Cyrus, conquered the greater part of the empire by 330 BC. Upon his death, most of the empire's former territory passed under the rule of the Ptolemaic Kingdom and Seleucid Empire, in addition to other minor territories which gained independence at that time. The Iranian population of the central plateau recovered power by the second century BC under the Parthian Empire.

BRINGING IN SOME GAME 

The snowstorm proved so severe that for three days the party at Professor Jeffer's cabin were completely stormbound. At one point Andy and Chet ventured out--in an endeavor to bring in the dead moose--but were unable to accomplish their object. 

During the time spent at the cabin, the boys became well acquainted with Barwell Dawson, and found the hunter and explorer a person much to their liking. Although he was rich and well educated, he did not act as though he considered himself above them. He took a lively interest in all they had to tell, and knew how to "draw them out," so that, almost before he was aware of it, Andy had related the details of his troubles with his shiftless Uncle Si and with the mysterious Mr. A. Q. Hopton. 

"More than likely that fellow, Hopton, will bear close watching," said Barwell Dawson. "If he is a sharper--and it looks as if he might be--he will try to swindle both you and your uncle. It was very unwise for your uncle to try to do business with him without seeing a lawyer." 

"Uncle Si wanted to get the money without my knowing it," answered Andy, bitterly. He was glad to open his heart to one who could understand him. 

"I believe you--and that is not to your uncle's credit. You say he is shiftless and lazy?" 

"Very--and everybody around here knows it." 

"Then he is not fit to be your guardian."

Story: Sarah's New Kitty

"Meow."

Sarah's eyes grew wide upon hearing the sound that proceeded from the basket her mother held. "Mama, what's that sound? "Sarah," her mother said, "remember I told you that maybe we can get a pet if you could take good care of it? Well, you're seven years old now and I think you're ready for a special present." Sarah's mother placed the basket upon the floor; Sarah sank upon her knees, a broad grin upon her face. She gently lifted the yellow kitty and held its soft little body to her own. Sarah gave the kitty a small kiss; then she rubbed its head and neck. Soon it began to make gentle sounds. "Why is the kitty making those funny sounds?" she asked her mother. "Oh, that's called purring. It's the sound kittens make when they're happy," her mother said. "Can I give it a name?" Sarah asked. "Sure. It's a girl kitty, but choose any name you like." her mother said. Sarah considered the matter as her mother obtained two small bowls and placed them upon the floor; then she put water in one bowl and kitten food in the other. "Okay, Sarah. Let's see if the kitty is hungry." Sarah set the kitty upon the floor, and it walked to the food bowl, where it speedily began to eat. Sarah laughed at the kitten and said, "I know. I'm going to name you Kitty."
